nameStory: The Painted Skimmer gets its artistic name from the beautiful amber and brown pattern decorating its wings, which look like they've been carefully painted with a fine brush. The combination of warm amber at the wing bases and tips, along with distinctive brown spots scattered across the clear sections, creates a masterpiece that sets it apart from other dragonflies.
description: The Painted Skimmer is a medium-sized dragonfly that's like a flying work of art over New England's waters. Growing to about 1.7 inches long, it's easily recognized by its stunning wing pattern of amber patches at the base and tip of each wing, decorated with brown spots throughout. The body features a distinctive white stripe along the sides near the head that transitions to bright yellow toward the tail, creating a beautiful gradient effect.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the signature amber coloring at both the base and tip of each wing, with brown spots scattered throughout the clear middle sections - no other skimmer has this exact combination

idTips.label: Body Stripe
idTips.description: Notice the lateral stripe running along the sides that starts white near the head and gradually becomes bright yellow toward the tail end

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized at about 1.7 inches long - not as hefty as the Great Blue Skimmer but more substantial than smaller pond skimmers

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Flies with the typical skimmer pattern of patrolling back and forth over water, often returning to the same perch on emergent vegetation

idTips.label: Wing Sound
idTips.description: Makes a distinctive rustling sound in flight due to the thicker amber sections of the wings catching air differently than clear wings

habitat: Look for Painted Skimmers around shallow, weedy ponds, slow-moving streams, and marshy areas with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They prefer waters with muddy or sandy bottoms and are often found in areas where water lilies and other floating plants provide good hunting perches.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but they're not yet at peak numbers. Early individuals may be seen patrolling quieter backwaters.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for Painted Skimmers, when they're most active and visible patrolling their territories over water. This is the best time to observe their distinctive wing patterns and mating behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline significantly by early fall, with only occasional stragglers visible on warm days. Most have completed their life cycle by this time.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - they overwinter as nymphs (juveniles) in the mud at the bottom of ponds and streams, waiting for spring warmth to trigger their emergence.

funFact: Despite being called 'uncommon,' Painted Skimmers are actually excellent indicators of healthy wetland ecosystems - their presence suggests that a water body has the perfect balance of plant life, water quality, and prey insects that many other species also depend on.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the Widow Skimmer, but the Painted Skimmer's amber wing tips are the giveaway - Widow Skimmers have dark wing bases but clear tips. Remember: 'Painted has amber paint on both ends, Widow wears black only at the shoulders.'
contextualKnowledge: The term 'skimmer' refers to their hunting style of skimming low over water surfaces to catch insects, rather than the high-flying behavior of darners. All skimmers belong to the family Libellulidae, which includes some of our most colorful and easily observed dragonflies.
compareHints: Among its Libellula cousins, the Painted Skimmer is unique for having amber coloring at both wing bases AND tips - the Twelve-spotted has clear wings with dark spots, the Widow Skimmer has dark bases but clear tips, and the Four-spotted has amber only at the wing bases. The body's white-to-yellow stripe is also distinctive among New England skimmers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Libellula cousins, the widow skimmer's wing bands are by far the boldest and most extensive - twelve-spotted skimmers have distinct spots rather than bands, while slaty skimmers lack the dramatic black markings entirely.

Among New England's skimmer species, mature male Slaty Skimmers are distinguished by their uniform slate-blue coloration, unlike the bold white patches of Widow Skimmers or the spotted wings of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.

Among its Libellula relatives, twelve-spotted skimmer is unique in having exactly three spots per wing - four-spotted has one large spot per wing, while widow skimmer has broad dark bands rather than distinct spots.

Among New England's Libellula skimmers, male Spangled Skimmers are the only ones with solid metallic blue coloring - Great Blue Skimmers have blue abdomens but different thorax colors, while Slaty Skimmers are more gray-blue.

Among its skimmer relatives, the four-spotted is distinguished by having the fewest and most clearly defined wing markings - just four bold spots compared to the twelve-spotted skimmer's busy pattern or the widow skimmer's broad white patches.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Great Blue Skimmer stands out for its large size and solid blue coloration without distinctive wing patterns.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Golden-winged Skimmer's amber wing patches set it apart from most relatives.
Among its Libellula relatives, Needham's Skimmer is distinguished by having dark wing bases without the white patches of Widow Skimmers or the multiple spots of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.
